name: Chloe Young

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm from the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, parties or government, and we sell nothing. Your answers are confidential, so tell me what you'd say aloud and what you think privately. What does a normal day at work look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Chloe, 27, lead property-claims clerk at a small insurer. I have a bachelor's degree and am good at spotting when a storm date, policy start and adjuster's note do not line up, though the pay is low for a lead. I use AI now and then for blank checklists, not customer files. I rent alone, have no children, and there are few similar jobs here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell neighbours that a storm claim still needs the date of the flood and what the policy actually covers. I lead a small property-claims paperwork team at an insurer, and I check water-damage photos against the adjuster's visit note before a payment letter goes out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If AI stays modest, my work probably stays. I'm 27 with a bachelor's degree and good at the files, but the insurer pays below other team leads, I have three weeks of rent saved and there are few similar jobs nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep checking basement-water claims against adjuster notes and policy dates. From the next pay, I'd cancel my 18 monthly game subscription and put that fee in a separate rent account; I might use AI now and then to draft a blank checklist, with no customer details.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about rent even in the quiet version. A broken boiler would use up most of my three-week cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What needed checking on the basement file?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A family sent photographs of a wet basement, but the storm date on the claim was two days after their policy started. I had the adjuster confirm the water line before we sent a letter that might have been wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your sister help with rent?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I rent alone and have no children. My sister lives nearby, but I would rather work from my own pay than count hers as a safety net.

I'd keep **payment letters** tied to the actual water line.
think: I have **three weeks saved** despite leading the claims paperwork team.
I earn **below lead pay** with few similar jobs nearby.
do: Keep **checking basement claims** against adjuster visits and policy dates.
Cancel **game subscription** and save its 18 fee from next pay.
Use AI on **blank claim checklists** without customer details, as I do now.
feel: **Anxious** about rent and a thin cushion before major AI change.
S0.quote: A broken boiler would use up most of my three-week cushion.
fieldNote: **Low lead pay** and three weeks saved explain anxiety despite strong claim-handling skill.
Her occasional AI use stays on **blank checklists**, while real payment letters need adjuster evidence.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI can read policy wording and draft a first claim letter, but it must not quietly turn a missing photo into a refusal. The person whose basement flooded needs a route to correct our file.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My team might shrink because much of our job is reading and answering claims. I'm good at the awkward files, but three weeks saved means even a small hours cut would put my rent at risk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the claims manager for paid time to compare the new AI letter check with twenty closed storm files, including the policy-start case and one clear covered claim. If the manager approves and the tool catches wrong dates without inventing exclusions, I'd use it for a week of draft letters with a named clerk checking each one; I'd defer buying a new bicycle until my hours are clear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about my hours, but I can run a fair test. A quicker refusal is not an improvement if the evidence was filed in the wrong tab.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What two outcomes should the test show?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The policy-start case must pause for a date check, while the covered claim should be paid rather than delayed. I'd mark both outcomes on paper before trusting a new letter draft.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why defer the bicycle?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My bicycle still works, though the gears slip. I can have it repaired instead of buying a new one while I wait for the staffing plan.

I'd test **policy dates** and covered files before live letters.
think: I could lose **paid lead hours** as reading and replies automate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AGI by 2028 could read and decide claim paperwork before inspection robots arrive around 2031. A claimant should still have a person to call about a wrong refusal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my team-lead post could be cut quickly if the insurer trusts cheaper claim decisions. My three weeks saved and the few local insurance vacancies would make a long search impossible without another wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd ask the local housing office and two insurers about actual paid casework or claims vacancies, wages, hours and start dates. If cut in the first year after 2028, I'd take a signed role whose wage covers rent, food and travel; for any unpaid gap I'd seek available paid shifts and speak to my landlord before rent is late, and if no role qualifies I'd keep searching paid work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about my own pay, though I can check real openings now. I know policy wording, but I cannot make the housing office create a paid desk for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could you show another employer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd show a hiring manager the storm-date correction with the family's name and address removed. It demonstrates why I asked for the adjuster's water-line note before refusing the file.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why do start dates matter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My rent is due on the first of the month. An offer starting six weeks later would still leave a gap, so I'd check start dates as well as annual salary.

I'd check **actual paid vacancies** before promising a fallback.
think: I expect **my lead post** could go quickly.
I cannot cover **rent** through a long search with three weeks saved.

Seek **paid shifts** through any gap or without a qualifying role; contact landlord before arrears.
feel: **Anxious** about a realistic lead-post cut and only three weeks of rent saved.
S2.quote: I cannot make the housing office create a paid desk for me.
fieldNote: **2028 thinking AGI** reaches claims paperwork before 2031 inspection robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years to 2031 gives time to check whether insurers still pay people to inspect damaged homes, not just read screens. Thinking AI reaches my claim paperwork then; inspection robots follow about 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could train as a field adjuster, but a bachelor's degree in another subject does not qualify me to estimate a damaged wall. I cannot pay course fees or lose wages to train when I only have three weeks saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the claims manager for the exact field-adjuster qualification, paid trainee vacancies and course funding. If a real paid place opens, the insurer funds the course on paid hours, and the training wage after any car costs covers rent, food and travel, I'd enrol and complete supervised visits before signing an estimate alone; in the first year after 2031 I'd take a signed adjuster post only if it still pays those bills, otherwise keep paid claims work while offered and seek other paid local work if cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, though five years lets me inspect a real training contract. A course certificate without paid site work would not cover my rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would supervised visits teach you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: An adjuster has to measure the water line and date the photographs while the claimant can explain what happened. I'd need supervised visits before signing an estimate on my own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you afford field travel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the trainee post requires a car, I would check its mileage payment and insurance before accepting. A wage that looks enough until fuel and cover are deducted is not enough.

I'd say **2031 thinking AI** reaches files before 2034 inspection robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade to 2036 gives me time to build more than three weeks of rent money, but thinking AI still reaches claims paperwork before inspection robots around 2039. I would not bet my whole career on reading forms faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I will be 37 then, not near retirement. I still have only three weeks saved now, so I cannot call the long runway safe unless my pay or savings actually change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the storm-date correction in my claim checklist and save the cancelled 18 game fee whenever I am paid, then review my rent and savings every six months. In the first year after 2036 I'd stay in paid claims work only while there are real hours; if those end, I'd seek a signed local job covering rent, food and travel, with no assumption that an adjuster post will exist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about present rent, though ten years gives me more chances to qualify for other work. I would rather see six months of actual savings than a ten-year plan on a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What stays on the checklist?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The checklist needs policy start, storm date and an adjuster's water-line note. A later clerk can see why the first letter was held.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your sister fund a buffer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My sister might share dinner, but her income is hers. The rent buffer has to come from my pay.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because the lead claims wage could disappear before another paid casework desk opens. Written cut notice, real vacancies with start dates and a landlord conversation before arrears would help me keep rent current.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what a denial letter feels like to the person holding it. A wrong storm date can turn a wet basement into an empty payment; I want the claimant to know how to correct the file.

headlineQuote: A wrong storm date can turn a wet basement into an empty payment; I want the claimant to know how to correct the file.
portrait: Chloe, **27**, leads property-claims paperwork after a bachelor's degree and checks storm dates against adjuster evidence.
Her **low lead pay**, rented flat, three-week cushion and few nearby insurer jobs make ordinary rent pressure serious.
She uses AI **occasionally** only on blank checklists and will trial letters on approved paid time with clerk review.
Fast 2028 AGI makes her **anxious**; another role needs a signed wage, checked start date and rent coverage.
She considers **field-adjuster training** only if the insurer funds paid hours and net wages after travel cover bills.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove her lead claims wage before another paid casework job appears.
whatWouldHelp: **Written cut notice**, real vacancy start dates and landlord contact before arrears would help.
